name: Chengdu Gourmet 2
review: Six-time James Beard-nominated chef Wei Zhu hails from Chengdu, in China’s Sichuan Province. Plan on visiting with a crew to forge a meal that combines Sichuan classics like mapo tofu, cumin lamb, and Chongqing crispy chicken with rarer finds such as their own Chinese sausage, green Sichuan peppercorn fish soup, and vinegary shoestring potatoes. The newer Chengdu Gourmet 2 location just north of Pittsburgh is more elaborately decorated (and features fresh fish and shellfish tanks) than the original Squirrel Hill branch.

name: Hyeholde Restaurant
review: When William Kryskill built the Hyeholde for his wife, Clara, 87 years ago, the area surrounding Pittsburgh International Airport was a vast stretch of farmland far from Downtown. Today, it’s suburbs, some fancy homes, and big box stores, yet the restaurant survives as a reminder of an era of white-tablecloth dining and formal service. Longtime chef Chris O’Brien purchased the castle-like restaurant from the Kryskill’s daughter Barbara a few years ago, carrying on the tradition of romantic dining with a bill of fare that includes sherry bisque, summer gazpacho, and elk loin with baby turnips, chard, and port au poivre sauce.

name: Alta Via (multiple locations)
review: Alta Via has two locations and a pizza offshoot, and is the latest offering from the city’s oldest restaurant conglomerate, Big Burrito Restaurant Group. Go here for satisfying pasta, salads, layered vegetable courses, and polished service.

name: Pusadee’s Garden
review: The owners of Pusadee’s Garden took a big risk when they closed their beloved, homestyle Thai restaurant for a few years to renovate the space from the ground up. The bet paid off — it’s been more than three years since the relaunch, and reservations can still be hard to come by (tip: they hold space for walk-ins; put your name on the waitlist, and you’ll likely get a table). This year, primary chef Bootsaba “Gik” Tongdee earned her first James Beard Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic semifinalist spot for her menu of multiregional Thai dishes. Pittsburgh architecture firm MossArchitects turned the multi-building space into a visual stunner, and the interior garden is now maturing into an escapist destination dining location.

name: The Allegheny Wine Mixer
review: Allegheny Wine Mixer is a Lawrenceville favorite, with its eclectic collection of flea-market paintings and a name inspired by the Catalina Wine Mixer scene in Step Brothers. As such, it doesn’t take itself too seriously, though it offers a selection of interesting wines by the glass, with pours from often underrepresented wine regions and a small but compelling cocktail list. Food is limited to meat-and-cheese plates, toasties, sweet bites, and specials like hot dog Sundays. Co-owner with Piccolo Forno’s Domenic Branduzzi, Roger Li also operates three nearby establishments: the excellent Izakaya Umami, multifaceted Nanban, and terrific Hong Kong-influenced Parlor Dim Sum. All are worth visiting.

name: Piccolo Forno
review: Long before Lower Lawrenceville was a mini-restaurant row, Piccolo Forno served Northern Italian cuisine to hungry diners. Domenic Branduzzi followed in his parents’ culinary footsteps when he opened the restaurant in 2005. It’s a destination for thin and crispy wood-fired pizza (try the speck e mascarpone and mortadella e pistachio) and pasta made from scratch by Branduzzi’s mother, Carla. Branduzzi’s fantastic grappa and amari bar Grapperia is just around the corner, a terrific spot for pre- and post-dining drinks.

name: Driftwood Oven
review: California-influenced baker’s style pizzas are the core of Neil Blazin’s sourdough shop in Lower Lawrenceville. He and his team offer square and round pies, plus Roman-style cuts of pizza ranging from classics to seasonal options such as corn and peach. Over the years, Blazin has expanded Driftwood Oven into a full-fledged bakery, with high-quality bread, bagels, and sweets. The menu also includes hefty sandwiches, salads, and snacks. Seating is limited.

name: Apteka
review: This pioneering restaurant has landed on the James Beard Award lists several times for good reason: The compelling vegan menu marries Eastern European cuisine with a deep embrace of Western Pennsylvania seasonality. Apteka’s beverage program is every bit as exciting as its culinary offerings; there’s a top-notch, largely Eastern Europe-focused natural wine selection, a strong cocktail list, terrific beer, and one of the best nonalcoholic drinks lists in town that includes a variety of homemade sodas. Get the nettle soup in season or the pickle plates; pierogies are always a win, as is the celeriac schnitzel.

name: Soju
review: Pittsburgh’s smaller, independently owned restaurants are often deeply personal endeavors. Soju, Simon Chough’s Korean-fusion restaurant in Garfield, takes that notion to the max. He offers an array of Korean dishes inspired by his grandmother’s recipe while weaving his distinctive touch through the menu with dishes such as galbi jjim morphed with elements of French onion soup like Hawaiian bread croutons and soulful kimchi jjigae with three versions of kimchi. When offered, Chough’s mandu are among the best dumplings in Pittsburgh. Cough extends the grace of the space to others through an ongoing series of pop-ups that allow Pittsburgh chefs to express their culinary voices.

name: Morcilla
review: Acclaimed restaurateurs Justin Severino and Hilary Prescott Severino founded Morcilla to follow their lauded, now-closed Cure. Sit in the taverna-style dining room for larger plates from executive chef/partner Nate Hobart, like top-notch Laurel Hill Farm trout with vivid salsa verde. Morcilla’s bar offers perfectly balanced cocktails, deep wine list, and an outstanding spirits selection.

name: Trace Brewing
review: What does the definition of a contemporary brewery look like? Visit Trace Brewing in Bloomfield. The taproom offers an ever-shifting mix of easy-to-love beer covering a wide range of styles and ABV percentage, as well as on-tap cocktails from nearby Goodlander Cocktail Brewery. By day, Trace showcases a top-tier coffee menu and doubles as an easy-breezy space for meetings and hanging out. The deliberately inclusive space hosts a range of events, including the super popular Slappers N Bangers, Disco Sunday Disco, and Sunday drag brunches. There’s almost always something tasty to eat, as Trace programs a deep rotation of the region’s food trucks.

name: Tessaro’s American Bar & Hardwood Grill
review: A Pittsburgh institution since 1981, Tessaro’s serves thick, handcrafted burgers with a custom blend of beef ground in-house daily cooked over a blend of PA hickory, oak, maple, and ash hardwoods by longtime grillmaster Courtney McFarlane. The tavern-style burgers are the primary draw, though you should also make it a point to visit the historic Bloomfield building on Thursdays for Tessaro’s weekly rib night. The menu is rounded out with steaks, chicken, and sides. Seating sprawls across several expansions; the best place to sit is still the front room, where you can enjoy a burger and cold beverage at or near the 1933 art deco Sears and Roebuck bar.

name: Fet Fisk
review: Fet Fisk, Pittsburgh’s buzziest new opening of 2024, debuted in March in a former Italian restaurant space in Bloomfield. Nik Forsberg, who landed a 2023 James Beard award semifinalist nod while operating Fet Fisk as a pop-up, helms the kitchen, offering a seasonal, Scandinavian-influenced lineup of dishes like pickled mackerel with smoked beets and seafood salad. The juicy roasted chicken with lingonberry sauce is a must.

name: Kelly’s Bar & Lounge
review: It’s increasingly rare to find a welcoming neighborhood bar that serves good food and well-made drinks at reasonable prices, yet maintains an old-school vibe without trying too hard. Kelly’s Bar & Lounge, founded in the 1940s and every bit as relevant today, is one of them. Grub highlights include a killer chicken sandwich, a tuna melt, and tofu bites. Cocktails veer toward staples like Negronis, palomas, and vespers, with daily specials rotated into the mix.

name: Showcase BBQ
review: Drew Allen has perfumed Homewood with the aroma of hardwood smoke and slow-cooked meat for over 20 years. His Showcase BBQ is a draw for its smoked ribs, which have a tender tug as you pull the just-charred meat from the bone. His melting turkey ribs (technically part of the shoulder) are a reminder that enjoying the great bird ought not to be limited to Thanksgiving. Top those, or the crisp chicken wings, with a spoon of Showcase’s piquant barbeque sauce to add a little oomph to your day. The sides here are as much of a draw as the meats — yams, green beans, mac and cheese, and potato salad are a few of the standouts.

name: Casbah
review: Casbah is a Pittsburgh classic in Shadyside that’s about to celebrate its 30th anniversary for good reason. It’s a crowd pleaser for tailored gatherings, with an engaging wine list, strong service, and the kind of meal to linger over. Start with dishes like Mediterranean spreads and grilled artichokes, move on to mussels or grilled octopus, split the chicken orecchiette with sage cream, or splurge on the Elysian Fields lamb.

name: Lilith
review: Jamilka Borges and Dianne DeStefano were two of the chefs who helped spur Pittsburgh dining forward in the 2010s. Last year, the duo paired up to open Lilith, a lovely neighborhood bistro carrying on the tradition of hospitality-focused, joyful dining in the space previously occupied by the late Toni Pais’ Cafe Zinho. Borges’ savory offerings tilt coastal, drawing influence from her native Puerto Rico with items like scallop crudo, coconut oil, chili, and lime. DeStefano handles the bakery side of the operation, offering a selection of fresh bread and classic-meets-contemporary desserts such as baked Alaska with creme fraiche semifreddo, plus strawberry, lemon, and coriander streusel.

name: Max’s Allegheny Tavern
review: Hit Max’s Allegheny Tavern in Pittsburgh’s East Allegheny neighborhood for a bit of history. The front room’s grand wood-paneled bar and hexagonal tiled floor date back to the early 1900s when the building was called Hotel Rahn. It has existed as Max’s since 1977, offering a sprawling series of semi-private nooks and dining rooms across the floorplan of two attached buildings. The portions of the German-style cuisine are hefty; try the schnitzels, sausages, and German potato salad.

name: DiAnoia’s Eatery
review: Pleasing breakfast, lunch, and dinner selections plus ultra-friendly service combine to make DiAnoia’s Eatery the day-into-night Italian restaurant that makes it a city staple. Breakfast means egg sandwiches, simple omelets, and toasts on terrific bread. Lunch is cold and hot paninis, pasta, and a few small plates. DiAnoia’s dinner menu expands on the pasta and contorni, adding larger dishes such as luscious porchetta and steak Florentine. Don’t skip the next-door pizzeria, Pizzeria Davide, and the family’s bakery and takeaway shop, Pane e Pronto, just a few blocks up the street.

name: Fig & Ash Wood Fire Kitchen
review: Corey Hughes and his team opened Fig & Ash in 2020 and today the handsome restaurant is an anchor of the revived Northside. Go here for vegetable-focused small plates and spins on traditional dishes — peach Caprese salad, summer squash crab cakes. Meaty mains feed a crowd, with items like short rib and pork belly meatloaf and a formidable pork shank.

name: EYV Restaurant
review: EYV chef and owner Mike Godlewski marries fancy techniques and plating with a seasonal menu that lets its ingredients shine. Vegetables take the stage at the forefront of most dishes, though meat can be used as an accent.

name: Bar Marco
review: Housed in a former firehouse, 12-year-old Bar Marco is one of the restaurants that pushed Pittsburgh’s restaurant revival forward in the early 2010s. The establishment pairs a well-executed Italian menu with pork tonnato, pastas, and fleeting seasonal offerings like asparagus with pistachio pesto and fava greens. The Strip District eatery has a top-flight cocktail list and one of Pittsburgh’s largest selections of amari. Bar Marco is a no-tip restaurant, with the two-course menu currently running $45 for an antipasti or salad and a pasta or large plate.

name: Balvanera
review: Pittsburgh native Meredith Boyle returned to the Steel City with her husband, Fernando Navas, in 2023 to open a bigger, glitzier version of Balvanera, the Argentine restaurant the couple has run in New York City since 2014. Navas offers gorgeously crafted versions of the South American country’s dishes that venture well beyond the signature grilled steaks (which are also terrific). Pastry chef Ginger Fisher Baldwin adds destination-worthy desserts to the chic experience.

name: Udipi Cafe
review: This suburban Indian restaurant is one of the region’s oldest vegetarian establishments. The bustling dining room at Udipi resembles a neighborhood diner, but instead of plates of eggs and hash browns, it’s an assemblage of dishes from southern India’s Tuluva-Mangalorean and Andhra cuisines. The main draws are dosas, fermented rice, and lentil batter griddled into yard-long crepes stuffed with potatoes, onions, and other ingredients. Sambahr (lentil and vegetable soup), deluxe thali platter, and chili padoka are among other favorite dishes.

name: Con Alma
review: Con Alma is a favorite downtown destination for pre- and post-show drinks and entertainment in a standalone space. The broad dining room and elegant bar harken back to an era when Pittsburgh was a hotbed for jazz. Today, you’ll find local and touring musicians playing here seven nights a week. Con Alma’s drinks menu features terrific seasonal cocktails, (spins on) classics, and a sharply curated wine list. The establishment’s dinner menu draws from Mediterranean influences, with roasted whole branzino with spicy berbere caponata, preserved lemon, and snacky bites like beet muhammara.

name: The Warren Bar & Burrow
review: The Warren is always there to fill our cravings after concerts, performances, and sporting events with a kitchen that stays open until midnight (a rare find in a town where it’s hard to get a good bite after 10 p.m.) and a bar open nightly till 2 a.m. You’ll find a selection of well-made, globally influenced pub grub as well as fresh fish and sushi dishes from business partners Penn Ave. Fish Co. The terrific bartenders seamlessly straddle high-volume and more elaborate cocktail styles and offer terrific beer and wine lists. The new sidebar, E.T.A. is a Japanese-style standing bar with an ace highball and cocktail list; the vinyl record playlist offers a significantly more chill atmosphere than its raucous neighbor.

name: Gi-Jin
review: The Richard DeShantz Restaurant Group operates numerous bars that happen to be restaurants throughout the city, ranging from the Strip District funhouse Coop de Ville to the eclectic Fish nor Fowl. The best is Gi-Jin. The intimate Downtown spot highlights raw fish with some of the city’s best nigiri, and its sushi chefs also prepare terrific hand rolls. Small plates such as hamachi crudo with ponzu, ginger oil, and daikon also stand out. Gi-Jin’s beverage list is deep, with sake and gin selections that are hard to find elsewhere in Pittsburgh.

name: Cafe Momentum
review: Cafe Momentum, a Downtown restaurant with branches in Dallas and Nashville, is a mission-driven restaurant that serves a great meal. The staff is composed of those seeking social justice through the workplace as well as at-risk youth who learn front- and back-of-house skills throughout a 12-month paid internship. The menu features a signature smoked and fried chicken, red snapper with squid ink, and seasonal salads.

name: Everyday Noodles
review: Pittsburgh was a xiao long bao desert until Mike Chen, the godfather of modern Chinese cuisine in Pittsburgh, opened Everyday Noodles in Squirrel Hill in 2013. The neighborhood is now a destination for regional Chinese dishes, with this foundational gem still putting out juicy soup dumplings and the “thwap! whap!” sounds of cooks pulling and stretching noodles for dishes like dan tzu noodles. Grab some items from the top of the list, too (the funky-sweet golden cabbage is a must-get).

name: Moonlit Burgers
review: Skip the national chains and head to one of Moonlit Burgers’ two locations for top-tier smash burgers, crispy chicken sandwiches, shoestring fries, and other tasty sides. Longtime Pittsburgh hospitality industry pros Mike McCoy and Derek Stevens spun an early COVID-19 era smash burger pop-up into a fully-fledged business in 2021, building the framework for a locally owned fast food destination — with a full bar to boot — in Dormont. Robust systems are on full display at Moonlit’s Uptown location before events and games at PPG Paints Arena, with the team keeping long lines moving and hot food delivered to tables at a quick clip.

name: Amazing Dumplings
review: The owners of Amazing Dumplings are a husband and wife team Fenping Geng and Feng Gao, who have deepened their celebration of Northern Chinese-style dishes for the past few years. Geng handles the dumplings, many of which come wrapped in vividly rainbowed, vegetable-dyed skins. Favorites include spicy pork with lotus root, the vivid “Van Gogh Starry Night” and sesame hot oil. Gao’s hand-pulled hot oil and biang biang noodles are also must-gets — the tomato and egg and the beef hot-oil version are great. Go with a group or a date.

name: Stuntpig
review: Ariel Alexander and Cody Maze launched Stuntpig as a food truck in 2020. Their celebration of smoked and cured meats (plus some vegetarian options) in sandwich form quickly became a sensation at Pittsburgh-area breweries and events. Earlier this year, the couple opened a brick-and-mortar version of the now-retired “Pig Rig,” serving a rotating menu of killer handhelds such as Mr. Orange (smoked chicken, peri-peri sauce, pickles), Pitt Beef (smoked and shaved beef, thin vidalia onions, tiger sauce) and Madonia’s Muffuletta. Expect a small selection of handmade sides. The super-herby potato salad is especially good.

name: Hidden Harbor/Independent Brewing Company
review: Just around the corner from Squirrel Hill’s primary business district is a two-for-one special: Hidden Harbor and Independent Brewing Company. Hidden Harbor is one of the foremost tiki bars in the country, featuring an array of potent, tropical-style cocktails (take the “shark fin” strength warnings seriously) and a rum collection of more than 500 bottles. Independent Brewing Company is focused on beer, serving an ever-rotating selection of local and international craft brews from its taps. Look for items like tacos al pastor and smash burgers on the food menu.

name: African Eats Cuisine
review: Look for meat pies and suya at this three-year-old Nigerian spot in Squirrel Hill from Dr. Saudat Lawal and her husband, Luke. Lawal brings the heat in the kitchen to her pepper soups (the transcendent fish pepper soup is a must-get), and her chicken drumsticks in red sauce are some of the best in town. Round out your meal with an order of fufu or jollof rice. Lawal and her family import peppers, spices, stockfish, and other ingredients harder-to-find in Pittsburgh to ensure the dishes are true to her memory. A menu of beer, wine, and cocktails like a Lagos sunrise is available in the comfortable dining room.

name: Dish Osteria & Bar
review: Michele and Cindy Savoia run the very definition of an Italian neighborhood restaurant just a few blocks from one of Pittsburgh’s main partying drags. Dish, a beloved favorite for over 20 years now, offers a Sicilian-influenced roster of dishes where high-quality ingredients take center stage. Start with seasonal soup and seafood dishes such as carpaccio di tonno and grilled sardines bathed in fresh lemon juice. Then dig into Savoia’s terrific pasta dishes like his celebrated rigatoni alla scamorza (with cheese). Brother Andrea Savoia runs the energetic front-of-house, where you’ll find regulars aplenty.

name: La Cocina de Betty
review: Maria Elizabeth “Betty” Hernandez, a native of Honduras, came to Pittsburgh in 2013 and launched her eponymous restaurant in Pittsburgh’s burgeoning Beechview neighborhood (home to many of the city’s most exciting Mexican, Central, and South American restaurants) in 2019. From a menu of Honduran, Salvadoran, and Mexican dishes, start with baleadas, the Honduran staple with homemade flour tortillas, refried beans, and fresh cheese, or Salvadorian pupusas with fried pork belly. The restaurant’s mammoth torta Cubana is one of Pittsburgh’s grand sandwiches.

name: Gab & Eat
review: Pittsburgh has plenty of old-school diners, yet Gab & Eat stands out. Owners Sue Smith and Karie Goedert manage the 41-year-old eatery with a welcoming, no-nonsense staff who cater to regulars and newcomers at the 14-seat counter or 12 booths in the rectangular space within a shopping plaza just outside the city limits. Enjoy a mug of robust coffee alongside fluffy pancakes, heaps of home fries, crispy bacon, and eggs cooked to your preference. Gab & Eat’s flattop chefs were smashing burgers long before it became trendy; the never-frozen beef patties, topped with razor-thin onions and traditional garnishes, rank among Pittsburgh’s finest.
